full_text:
Interviewer:	OK, when did you start your placement?

Subject:	Um, end of June, 28th June.

Interviewer:	So you’ve been here a fair while now.

Subject:	Yeah, I’ve just actually put in a letter to, er, to extend it, because I should finish the end of June but I want to work through the Summer as well, so hopefully I’ll finish end August time.

Interviewer:	So you’re enjoying it then?

Subject:	Yeah, I’m getting on with it all.

Interviewer:	Can you tell me a bit about the company that you’re working for?

Subject:	Yeah, it’s um, [company], it’s a subsidiary of [company 2] who are really well known, it’s a really big construction firm, and [company] are basically the, um, it’s a (multi-d?) consultancy and it was produced when [company 3] was privatised originally. So there’s offices – obviously we’ve got the architects in [town], we’ve got engineers in [town], um, we’ve got Scottish offices and we’ve also got the main office which is in [town], and it’s just engineers, architects and M&E. We do a lot – we mainly, um, public works, we mainly work on things like prisons, schools, stuff like that, although we do some development projects.

Interviewer:	OK, how would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	Um, very good actually. Um, it’s quite surprising really because I always thought I’d be coming into mainly an all-male environment but there’s actually – I’m one of four women in this office, and I think there’s 10 of us. We’ve got two interiors and then the PA as well, but I think it’s very – I don’t think it came into it really. (Yeah) But yes, I think it’s very positive, its like getting women involved in it.

Interviewer:	We’ll probably talk about that later on, but how useful do you think that your degree has been so far to the work that you’re doing?

Subject:	Um, I’m still – I’m still learning. It’s quite nice when, I remember, because there’s a couple of times it’s happened where I’m given something to do and I’m actually like, I can actually do this, I’ve actually been taught how to do something. But to be honest, at the moment I think it’s still in the very basic stages. But I’m in a situation where I sit near two of the architectural technicians and they’re lovely, they’ll just let me sit and ask them questions and I’ve got my little notebook that’s now jammed full of notes and things like that. And to be honest I think it’s more the other way around. I think working this year will help my degree loads because I think I’ll be able to go back into my final year and I will have learned quite a lot so I’ll be able to use it in final year projects and stuff like that. But yeah, I think the more management side of my course has played a part when I’ve been going to do drawing records, drawing [issue?], things like that, so yeah, I think it’s helped.

Interviewer:	OK. Is there anything that you wish you particularly had learned at uni before you started the placement?

Subject:	Yeah, it’s basically technical detail but to be honest I don’t – I think that’s something you learn as you’re working, I don’t think they could sit and teach us all the different little bits and pieces. And because my course covers – because it’s architectural engineering and management – covers such a wide range of stuff, I don’t think they can focus on the little areas, and so I think that once again working’s helped because it’s able to highlight the areas that I’m not so good at. But then to be honest I think if we were covering every single part of like technical aspects of the building and things like that, we’d just like be at uni for years.

Interviewer:	OK, were you taught about anything about health and safety at uni?

Subject:	Yeah, I had a health and safety course.

Interviewer:	Was that useful?

Subject:	Well it was health and safety within construction. To be honest I’ve only been on two site visits and we were immediately given all the correct PPE and stuff like that, so it’s mainly office-based health and safety that we’re having to consider. And because we’re a subsidiary of [company 2] we get all their health and safety drives coming through, so we all get these awareness weeks and stuff like that and they’re big on it because within the construction industry health and safety’s so – such a tricky area. But, um, when I had my module of health and safety, that was mainly within the construction industry and to be honest here we’re more focussed with designing for health and safety. But yes, it has helped.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that university could have done anything else to prepare you for the placement?

Subject:	Um, no, not really. The preparation was really good because we had a whole work book of stuff to do, but no – I think, I think it all depends on – I’ve been really lucky with my placement because I’ve come into an environment that’s so open and friendly, and they’ve got me – literally on my first day they already had me working on a project and I had it in my head that I’d be filing for a couple of weeks. And I’m so comfortable, I’m comfortable enough to ask if I’m stuck on something to go over and ask, and if I don’t understand they’ll sit there and actually take the time out to explain it to me. So I don’t know whether other people have different opinions on it but I think uni prepared fine, because I didn’t know what to expect when I first, when I first started, but I had all the paperwork in place and like I just gave it a go.

Interviewer:	OK, before you started, did the university or your department say what they hoped you’d get out of the placement?

Subject:	Yeah I think they wanted us to – it was an experience thing – and also a lot of people have found it – it’s going to be very beneficial when they actually go to get a job after they graduate, because they’ll have this experience which is one over. Because it’s kind of tricky getting a job and I think it’s one over people who haven’t had the experience. I know what it’s like to work in an office environment where we’ve worked under pressure, where we’ve worked through quite a few problems and stuff, so I think it’ll help. And yeah, I think – I think it’s generally sort of beneficial.

Interviewer:	OK. How have you found the transition from education to work? 

Subject:	Besides being permanently shattered?

Interviewer:	That’s quite a big thing …

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Not just the technical side of doing the work but it’s quite a big thing just having to get up in the morning …

Subject:	Yeah it’s really hard. Um, actually the working part of it I don’t have a problem with at all, I actually really enjoy it, and especially because I’m still learning. The only part of it is the social that I have a problem with, not being able to go out, but then I think it’s nice because I have far more independence and things like that because I’ve got – because I’m earning money and things like that, so, I think it’s been fairly smooth although I am quite looking forward to going back to uni next year.
Interviewer:	Have you felt that you’ve had to face any new issues like office politics or dealing with the boss or clients?

Subject:	Not in particular, no. Because it’s such a sort of – it’s quite a laid back environment. It’s like, you have the work to do and as long as you achieve it well and achieve it in time… And you’ve got a lot of support from the people around you, so if you – like I said earlier – if I’m particularly stuck on an area I feel comfortable enough to tell people and there aren’t really … Because it’s such a small environment, if anyone has a problem we just discuss it because we have weekly meetings and things like that. So there aren’t a lot of conflicts in that respect.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. Do you think that university and work have different goals and priorities?

Subject:	Mm. I don’t know. I think that the thing I’ve found a little bit tricky with work is that I don’t have set targets – you know with uni how you’re just working to your final exams or you’re just working to get the piece of coursework done. Work, it’s like a day by day basis and so I mean if I’ve got stuff to do I have to write it down, I have to have like my little targets for the day, because otherwise I don’t really have a focus, and I end up going off at a tangent doing completely the wrong job or something like that. But I think, um, yeah, I think uni’s better in that respect because you’re working, you’re always working towards the goal of exams and things like that. But then it’s easier on yourself at work because at the end of the day you go home and you’re home, really, whereas at uni you’ve permanently got your exams on your mind and stuff like that. So, yeah, I think, I think working’s nicer because you don’t have that permanent pressure and stuff like that, so.

Interviewer:	OK, does the company have a specific structure or programme in place for placement students?

Subject:	Um, no. I think they have the set training and things like that, but I don’t think they do – because I remember when I went for my interview – because we’ve got another placement student in and she’s an interior architect – and I spoke to people before, and they’ve always taken on a student for a placement but they’ve only ever done interior people and it’s the first time they’ve actually taken on an architectural engineer. And so, um, I think it’s like, they’re just playing it by ear, they didn’t know what skills I’d be coming in with and I think, um, they’re just sort of taking it step by step. I mean I have my appraisals and things like that, but I don’t think there’s a particular structure for – I just jumped straight into a project which is nice, so. I don’t think there is a particular structure no.

Interviewer:	OK. It sounds like it’s going quite well anyway do you think there’s a need to have a structure or anything at all?

Subject:	Um, no. Because if I ever needed to query anything it was, I was comfortable enough to say something so.

Interviewer:	OK. What does your job entail doing?

Subject:	I don’t think I have a specific role. I do bits and pieces, like, um, I just sort of – because we’re working on a major project at the moment, I’m just given little bits and pieces to do. Um, it’s varied from drawing issue, management side of things, right through to sort of more technical stuff. I’ve been working on some sub-stations at the moment. But there’s no particular focus or role at the moment. But then to be honest at the start of it I said to my boss, you know, who unfortunately isn’t here, I said to him, look, this year is for actually like discovering what I want to do when I actually graduate, because I love all aspects of my course, I didn’t have a particular focus. And I mean I’ve been here six months now and I’m already focussing towards the management side of things. But it’s nice because I’m getting lots of different tastes of lots of different things, so I don’t have a particular role.

Interviewer:	So has it been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	I think it’s exceeded my expectations a little bit because I didn’t think I’d be given the responsibility I’ve been given. I think it’s been good in that respect because I honestly thought when I first joined I’d just be like learning the ropes, I wouldn’t be given like very much responsibility, and it was nice being able to get straight stuck in and stuff like that, so, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility though?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. I mean sometimes I’m a little bit funny about having to issue some important drawings or things like that, but as I said earlier, I’ve got people around me all the time so I’m able to just OK it with them and stuff like that. But no it’s nice having that responsibility, and people have a bit of faith in you.

Interviewer:	But feeling supported at the same time?

Subject:	Definitely, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, how would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

Subject:	It’s been really – it’s been a total learning experience. I mean there isn’t a day that goes by when I haven’t like learned something new and have to jot it down in my little book. My book is so thick now it’s ridiculous. I think I forgotten …

Interviewer:	It’s like your bible?

Subject:	It so is as well. And also CAD as well. I wasn’t so good on CAD when I first joined, but because I’m literally on it every day now, um, I – the one thing I’m really looking forward to going back to uni with is the fact that when we do our final year project I’ll be able to actually produce all my drawings on CAD, so, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, so what would you say have been the best and worst things about the placement so far?

Subject:	Um, the best thing was when – is, I think it’s the level of responsibility that I get. Because like I’ve got quite a lot of trust which is really nice. It’s like when we had a particular bid going out for a job and it was quite sort of, it was majorly under pressure, and the guy that I was working for sort of said, oh, I’m actually away on the day that all the drawings have got to be issued, and this was the end of the summer, I’d only been there a couple of months, and they’d let me – I had to issue all the drawings. Which at the end of the day I was like, oh I was shaking by the end of the day because I was like, if this goes wrong it’s all my fault. But it’s nice, no, because, like I had everyone around me so if I said I was a bit unsure I could ask. And so I’d say that was definitely the best part. And to be honest I quite enjoy it when I’m working under pressure. Um, the worst bits – um, are probably in the lulls when there isn’t that much to do because, I mean I try and find things to do but sometimes it can be a little bit slow. But it’s always going to be like this in this industry because you’ll have like loads and loads of work on at one stage and then it just goes quiet for a month or so. But, and then also permanently being tired.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement then? Is it all positive?

Subject:	No I’d say it’s all pretty much all positive, because I’m hoping that I’m going to go back to uni – well I don’t which way it’ll work, I’ll either go back to uni and become like more mature, or go back to uni and become a fresher again. But I think I – I’m actually quite looking forward to uni. Not to go back and see all my friends and stuff like that, but also to go back and actually use what I’ve learned, because I have been quite surprised how much I’ve learned actually. It’s great when actually you sit there and you, you’re working through a particular problem and you’re like, I’m sure six months ago I didn’t know how to fix this, and now I do, so. All in all it’s been such a learning experience I think it’s – and also you – I don’t know – working in an environment like this also changes your outlook. Because team working as well, like, sometimes when you’re at uni you don’t, you usually have to work individually on projects or you’re very very focussed, whereas this you have to consider all the people around you, what are they working on, how’s it going to affect what you’re working on and stuff like that, so.

Interviewer:	I was going to ask you about teamwork actually.

Subject:	Oh right, I’m getting ahead of myself.

Interviewer:	That’s OK. Did you do quite a bit of teamwork at uni as well?

Subject:	Yeah we did a few group projects and things like that.

Interviewer:	How do you think doing teamwork at work compares to doing teamwork at uni then?

Subject:	I think it’s better, because here you’re doing a job and you’re paid to do the job, and you – most people really enjoy what they do. Whereas at uni you always get the odd few who are along for the ride and stuff like that, so I think here, even if someone doesn’t particularly want to do a part of it, they’ll put their all into it anyway, and it can be – you know you have an outcome to it. It’s like, coursework’s great and everything but you don’t – you get a mark at the end of it for all this work you’ve done, whereas teamwork here you end up coming out with, I don’t know, part of a building at the end of working through it, so it’s …

Interviewer:	It’s seeing something more physical at the end then?

Subject:	Mm, I think so. I think – also there’s a bigger age range here, there’s lots more experience, and we’re all a bit sort of cocky and young at uni and think we can get away with it and stuff, so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it is worthwhile doing group work at uni then?

Subject:	I think so, yeah, definitely, because – I mean a few people that I work with, especially when we do, um, coursework with other courses, I think that really helps. Because I had to do some coursework with a couple of civil engineers and the technical stuff I was absolutely useless on but they were really good on. Whereas the management side of things, the organised time side of things, I was better on. So it’s great because you actually bring in all these different elements and so, um, yeah I think it’s definitely beneficial. The only problem I have is the way they put the teams together. Because they just stick you in alphabetical order and stuff so you end up working with the same people over and over, so. But it’s definitely beneficial.

Interviewer:	OK, would you say that you have changed personally as a result of doing the placement?

Subject:	I think a bit of both really. I think, I don’t know …

Interviewer:	Has it made you, like, more confident? You were saying earlier that you feel more independent as well.

Subject:	Mm, I think so. It’s given me, I think it’s given me better people skills, especially when you get someone you’ve never spoken to before ring you up because they’re on site and they need you to explain. Like earlier I had a guy ring me up that I’ve never spoken to before and he wanted me to explain a dimension that had just been basically been put on the wrong angle, and it was just – you get the information out as quickly as you can but in a polite and nice way, kind of thing. And I think my people skills have grown quite a bit. I think I have become more confident as well, whereas I think at uni, I mean you could just end up staying with your little clique and you don’t really, um, but yeah – I think, I think it’s been placement-based, my changes, but I think they would have happened anyway.

Interviewer:	OK, did you say that there was another student on placement here? Have you found that helpful at all or …?

Subject:	Yeah we’re working in different – we’ve worked on a few things together but we’ve worked in different areas, because she’s an interior architect, but we have worked on a few bits and pieces together. And I think it’s nice knowing someone’s going through the same thing, kind of thing. Yeah, I think that’s been helpful as well.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel like you’ve been treated like a permanent member of staff then?

Subject:	Yeah, I mean apart from a few odd bits, like, because we moved to the new office we needed new, new, um, first aiders and things like that, and to be honest that was one of the things I would have really gone for, but because…

Interviewer:	You’re not going to be here … 

Subject:	Yeah, there’s no point. And, um, things like training for the long term, like they won’t send me on massive training courses because they know I’m going to go in a few months. But besides that I feel like I’m sort of permanently here and sort of included …

Interviewer:	So, more within your actual team?

Subject:	Mm, definitely, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, when you’ve done teamwork, is there anyone that you’ve particularly liked or disliked working with?

Subject:	Um, not – I wouldn’t say anyone I’ve disliked. I particularly get on with the two architectural technicians which I sit next to, simply because they’re so easy-going that, like, if I’m, if I am stuck I feel totally comfortable, and they’ve always taken the time to help me as well. And also if I’ve finished a particular project and no-one else told me what to do, I can go to them and they’ll let me help them, you know, up to the level that I can, but… Also one of them, when we were – there was a Scottish prison that they needed help on so they sent me and the other architectural technician as well up there – so I get on with them really well.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been given a mentor at all in the company?

Subject:	Um, no. I think my boss is really – he’s the one that sort of goes through all the appraisals and things with me, and he’s off on site today but he’s like, really sort of laid back and if I had a problem I know I could probably go and talk to him. And he checks in with me now and then, just check and see what I’m working on. And he’ll give me little jobs to do as well. So, no, I don’t think – I could understand people needing one if it was a much bigger – bigger, like company, and bigger – um, environment to work in, but to be honest with such close knit group I don’t think we really need one.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. What do your appraisals involve then?

Subject:	Oh, I just had a three month one – which is basically covering, I think it’s like 10 different headings on, um, different aspects – things like teamworking and things like that, and then it’s just how I’m doing, and it’s just – I think it goes into what is required from me in the next 6 months. But the 3 month and the 6 month ones were – like because everyone who starts at the business gets two, like, how are you doing forms to fill in, up until 6 months, and after you’ve done that it’s just yearly after that. But, it was just things like, what plans are for the future and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	Sort of setting a target?

Subject:	So it’s nice because my boss said that he was putting a note on there to keep in contact with me in my final year, and if I’m still interested he’d be willing to sort of take me on after I’ve graduated as well.

Interviewer:	Do you think you will be interested in doing that?

Subject:	I think so, especially because, if I went into a small private company I don’t think I’d have the opportunities that I’d have, because you’ve got [company] and then you’ve got [company 2]. I think I can (inaudible) give me a better opportunity to actually like grow through the company and, and I don’t know, I can’t think that far ahead.

Interviewer:	So even though it’s like a small placement, you’re part of a big …

Subject:	There’s so many connections, yeah. And so it’ll be nice knowing that if I do want to go and focus on the design management side of things I can go off in that direction, and if I want to go in another direction – and also they’re very big on like sponsoring to do Masters and stuff like that, because like the head of architecture who interviewed me, he’s in the middle of doing Masters and there’s – just something like one night a week – but they’re sponsoring him through that. So I think they’re quite big on the training and stuff like that, so I’d like to come back because I know there’s a lot of opportunities for me.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you fancy doing a Masters then?

Subject:	I don’t know. I’m not entirely sure. Because I’m still not completely sure on what focus I’m going on, although I am veering towards design management, I would like to go and do a Masters in something like that and just sort make it more sort of specialist, but, I’m keeping my options open.

Interviewer:	Is there anyone in the company that you’d regard as a role model at all?

Subject:	Um, I’m quite – it sounds really daft, I’m glad he’s not here – I quite like the job my boss does actually. So I kind of look up to him because like I think I’d be quite good at that. That’s awful isn’t it? I want my boss’s job! No, but I look up to him a lot. He’s very good at business development, the business development side of things. And also the other guy who’s actually a senior architect, he, um, he’s actually running this huge prisons project at the moment and, it’s just like, you sit and listen to him and he knows so much stuff, but I’m like, I just want to be like that, I just want to have that sort of knowledge on a particular area and just be, like, one of the best in my area, kind of thing. But there’s loads of different people I think, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, has anyone from uni been to visit you yet?

Subject:	Yes, I’ve had my tutor visit me once so far. 

Interviewer:	Did they tell you the reason that they were visiting you?

Subject:	Um, I think we get two visits and the first one is just literally to come and see how we’re getting on, and I put all the stuff that I’d been working on and just show her how I was getting on and she had a quick look through my diary and stuff, and she just wanted to make sure that I was on track for my – because you had to do a tech report at the end of it and she said, oh have you got a few titles, and I explained what I was planning on doing. And then she said well if I can work on it up until about Easter time, she said around Easter time, it’ll either be her or someone else coming to visit me just to see how I’m getting on with my report. So it was just kind of casual and she had a chat with my boss as well to see how I was getting on. So, yeah, it was just – it was kind of casual but it’s nice knowing that someone was really bothered about what I’m up to.

Interviewer:	So do you have to do this report for like the past year?

Subject:	Yeah, we have to do loads of different things. We have to complete a diary of every day, and my boss signs it every month. Um, we do a report on a particular subject which affects us, so whatever. Um, the portfolio I think involves your diary and then you keep like photos. I’ve only been to site a couple of times but I’ve been able to see elements of design, so I’m like standing there in a hard hat pointing, and um I think a poster, and there’s loads of different elements, but it’s just basically on a pass or fail situation. But it’s nice because I know that I’ll probably finish end of summer and then we’ve got about a month before we go back to uni, but I want to try and get it sorted before then so I can bring it in and people can – because I know people will check it here and stuff like that for me, which is nice, so yeah, the report’s the big part really.

Interviewer:	OK, would you be happy to go to your tutor if you did have a problem here?

Subject:	I think so yes, definitely. Either the tutor that visited or, um, [placement coordinator] who actually runs the whole thing. Because I’ve always got the impression he’s quite – if I went to him with a problem he’d try and sort it out. But yes, either one I’d probably go to quite happily. But if I had a problem here to be honest I don’t think I’d actually have an issue with going to my boss about it or going to anyone here.

Interviewer:	You’d try and sort it out here, yourself?

Subject:	I mean I’ll probably let them know I’m having a bit of an issue, but at the moment I’d try and sort it out myself first, because I’m so comfortable here I don’t think it would be a problem.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s good. Do you know if there is a complaints procedure either here or at uni if there was something …?

Subject:	Um, yeah, there is – it’s actually an email just went because we’ve got such a good intranet site there’s lots of links to things like support services, I think it’s called support services and it’s there if you need to talk to someone anonymously and get a bit of advice. There’s a situation (inaudible) that’s the one thing about [company 2] being so big, is that it’s got such a wide spectrum of services and, um, there is definitely a support services system. But as I said, I don’t think I really feel the need to go to them because we’re so close knit – I mean if it wasn’t my boss I’d talk to, I’d talk to someone in the office about it.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are appropriate facilities for women here?

Subject:	Yeah. Because before we moved in, the interior designer here designed it, so – and she’s a lady, so yeah, absolutely fine.

Interviewer:	What about when you’ve been on site and things like that?

Subject:	Oh no, no, not at all. And also, it’s so like because I’ve only been twice, but both times I had to sort of climb up and about and stuff like that and it’s like, double-takes by the builders as they’re looking at me, it’s like, it’s a woman, ooh, what’s she doing here? And, um, but no I’ve never really wanted to use the facilities on site to be honest. But no, I wouldn’t say – I still think they’re very very focussed on male environment on building sites simply because you don’t get a lot of women brickies and sort of women construction workers, so.

Interviewer:	So are you like comfortable going on site then or…?

Subject:	Yeah because I’m still in the excitement stage really about going on site, I’m just so keen to get on there, whereas I think if you talk to, like my friend [name] who does civil engineering…

Interviewer:	I’m going to see her on Wednesday.

Subject:	I think she’ll probably have a right rant. We sometimes ring each other during lunchtimes and she’s freezing on site covered in mud and I’m like, nice and cosy in an office. And I think it would be different perspectives from the girls that are actually on site, because they’ll be surrounded by lots of mud and dirt and things like that and they’ll be, I think they’ll have a completely different view. I’m sort of like quite lucky with my view of things at the moment, so.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think then that there have been any occasions when you feel like your gender has determined a reaction from some people or the outcome of things?

Subject:	Um, no – I think you still get the sort of like little bit of surprise, especially from the people on site when they, because I remember it was the other day - I’d done this drawing but I sign my name as C Brown so they don’t know I’m a girl. I rang up and he was asking (inaudible) to do with some bracing and he rang up and he said I need to speak to C Brown. I went, speaking, and he went, oh, um, hello. It’s just there’s still a bit of surprise, I think they’ve been sort of – especially project managers and stuff like that – they get more and more used to it. But I wouldn’t say – I think it must have but to be honest I haven’t experienced it that much, and, um – no, I wouldn’t say it’s affected you too much from gender but I’m, I’m probably being completely naïve. I think, um, when I went for my interview to work here when I was chatting to the head of architecture, he’s a lovely bloke, but he said, I quite like having girls in the office, and I thought, excuse me, and he’s like, no, it just brings out a nice balance. But even then he was obviously, like, swinging it slightly there, he wanted a balance in the office. 

Interviewer:	If you go somewhere else to work when you finish, would you consider things like the gender proportions in the office?

Subject:	Probably. Well I don’t know actually, because it’s never really bothered me that much because I know I’m the only girl on my course, I don’t really think about it. I wouldn’t actually – it wouldn’t deter me from going, working in an all-male environment would really bother me. If anything it’d probably make me slightly more, um, eager to prove myself because, you know, yeah, I think I’d probably be slightly more determined. It’s like, with my course I think I’m definitely out there to prove myself, especially now I’m now the final girl. I think …

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s because you feel like you have to, or is that just …

Subject:	I think it’s a personal thing. I think it does prove my point. No, also, there were 3 girls to start with and the 2 girls have dropped out now. And if it was anyone else, if it was a boy and a girl or 2 boys it wouldn’t have made a difference, but it’s the fact that I’m the only girl left now. And also I surround myself with – 2 of my best friends are in engineering and they’re really quite feisty, and so I think – I think no matter how much we say, oh, it’s getting better, I think we’re still out there to prove a point, because there’s still people, especially in this industry, that, um, aren’t willing to accept girls. It’s the way they’ve been taught and stuff like that, but I think me going out there to prove myself to my course and things like that, it obviously sets myself a bit of a challenge. It gives me my goals and my targets, so, I think probably a little bit of both, trying to do it for myself but also get one over them.

Interviewer:	So do you think that your career ambitions have changed or developed from doing the placement?

Subject:	I think they’ve developed because I think it’s highlighted areas that I wasn’t particularly bothered about while doing my course. Like I wasn’t – we were having the modules and things like that and I wasn’t really that bothered, but especially management, I didn’t – some of the modules I didn’t actually enjoy that much, it was more the architecture side of things. But coming into this, I’ve realised I like the architecture side of things but I’m actually focussing more on the management, so I think I’ll go back into my final year making a whole load more effort with the management side of things. Because I know, I know I’m quite good at it now, I’ve realised that I’ve got a little bit of a flair for it, which wouldn’t have been showing if I hadn’t done the placement, so, I think, yeah, it’s probably going to affect my final year quite a lot.

Interviewer:	OK, what about when you start work after you finish university, do you think the placement experience will help you?

Subject:	Yeah, because – well especially if I come back here – I think they’re probably more likely to see that I’ve got sort of sticking power and so they’ll be able to train me up and stuff like that and, um, yeah.

Interviewer:	You’ll settle in quicker and things like that?

Subject:	I think so, I think it’ll be nicer because I think, I presume, people will still be here that I know, and if I did go somewhere else I’d know what it would be like working in an environment like this, and so I think it would definitely benefit – it’s going to be beneficial to me in the end.

Interviewer:	OK, I’ve got some questions now that are questions that I asked you last time.

Subject:	Right. God I’ve got an awful memory.

Interviewer:	It’s not a test, it doesn’t matter what you said last time, it’s just seeing if the placement has made you change what you think.

Subject:	OK. I can’t remember what I said.

Interviewer:	What five words would you use to …

Subject:	 (inaudible) say what sorry?

Interviewer:	Describe your field of engineering or architecture and site management?

Subject:	Describe the field? I don’t know. Um, five words. Um. I suppose, you want like little sort of phrases like that? I suppose it’s very, um … give me a minute, hold on. Um, I’d say team working is very important, I’d say that organisation is really really important, especially with drawing issues and stuff like that, um, I suppose you’re focussing on my course though aren’t you? Um … I don’t know. Can you give me an example?

Interviewer:	Things like challenging?

Subject:	Oh right, OK. Um, can I use that one? Um, it is, um, it’s incredibly interesting as well, when you look at all the different aspects of the course, it’s um …

Interviewer:	So its very varied. Is it, even the work that you’re doing here is quite …

Subject:	Oh yeah, definitely, I’m getting a lot of um, a lot of experience. Probably another point as well, it’s given me a lot of experience, it’s given me a lot of confidence, and I’m able to go away and I’ve learned a lot, quite a lot. That’s not really five words but … 

Interviewer:	What would you say are the main advantages and disadvantages to being a woman in engineering?

Subject:	Um, I suppose some – when you look at some of them they can be advantages and disadvantages. Like women, although we try not to say it, we’ve still got quite a long way to go, we’ve still got quite a few points to prove, and that can be looked on as an advantage or as a disadvantage. Like people’s attitudes towards women. I think, um, another thing is, maybe a disadvantage is still the way people perceive women when it comes to engineering. Like the guy on the phone who said, oh, it’s a girl. He didn’t say it but you could really hear it in his voice. So when he asked me the question I really wanted to get it right. Um, I think it’s still quite surprising for people when – especially if you talk to like a senior engineer, a senior woman in a certain position as well, I think that can be an advantage because I think people are sort of maybe slightly wary so they’re more open up to new ideas and things like that. But I think there are so many points that can be made like that, that can be seen as disadvantages as well, it can swing both ways, so. I don’t think there’s any major advantages to being a woman but then I don’t think there’s any major disadvantages.

Interviewer:	OK, do you still think that women should be encouraged or enabled to do engineering?

Subject:	Mm, definitely. I think, um, well – I can’t remember whether I said this last time – I was in an environment where they wouldn’t have dreamt of suggesting engineering to me, it’s off my own bat that I’ve found out about it, and also my dad’s an engineer and dad’s side of the family is very engineering-focussed, and so I knew about my dad’s course and thought, well I kind of like architecture but I don’t think I can hack the 7 years, and I kind of stumbled across it. And also I’d heard about it because [university’s], you know, my dad said [university] is, well …

Interviewer:	Renowned?

Subject:	Yeah, renowned for its engineering. When I tell people I go to [university] they say, do you do sport? No, I don’t do sport. No, I don’t think – I definitely think there should be more, not necessarily encouragement but awareness that there are, you know, women can go into engineering, it’s not like a really blokey subject. The way women think as well, I think it would be helpful if women went into engineering, because men and women do think completely differently and I think to get a woman’s spin on certain ideas and certain ways of thinking I think would be great. It would be really good if women could be aware that they can get into this kind of career.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s everything.

Subject:	Is it that was quick.

Interviewer:	Thanks very much, that’s very helpful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when did you start your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, end of June, 28th June.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’ve been here a fair while now.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’ve just actually put in a letter to, er, to extend it, because I should finish the end of June but I want to work through the Summer as well, so hopefully I’ll finish end August time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’re enjoying it then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’m getting on with it all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer

turns.speaker: Subject

So there’s offices – obviously we’ve got the architects in [town], we’ve got engineers in [town], um, we’ve got Scottish offices and we’ve also got the main office which is in [town], and it’s just engineers, architects and M&E. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, very good actually.
